analysis.one_liner: Limits the number of patents drug makers can use in lawsuits to block cheaper biosimilar competitors.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the bill without opposition in July 2026, but the House has taken no vote on it since receiving it.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company wants to sell a cheaper copy of a biologic drug (called a biosimilar), the original maker often sues using stacks of dozens or even hundreds of patents, which can delay the cheaper version for years. This bill says the original maker can generally use no more than 20 patents in such a lawsuit, with courts allowed to allow more for good cause. Cheaper copies of expensive biologic drugs — used for cancer, arthritis, and other serious conditions — could reach patients sooner. The Senate passed the bill unanimously in July 2026, but the House has held it without a vote since then.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take expensive biologic drugs gain if cheaper biosimilars reach the market sooner, since biosimilars typically sell at substantially lower prices. Biosimilar manufacturers also gain, because a smaller patent list means shorter, cheaper litigation before their products can launch.

how_it_helps.text: Caps at 20 the number of listed patents a brand manufacturer can assert against a biosimilar applicant in an infringement lawsuit, with no more than 10 coming from later-issued patents.
Targets patents filed more than four years after the original drug's approval and manufacturing-process patents, the building blocks of patent thickets.
Lets a court raise the cap only when the interest of justice or good cause requires it, such as when the biosimilar applicant withholds required information.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name biologic drug manufacturers bear the cost: with fewer patents available in lawsuits, they face earlier loss of exclusivity and less revenue from keeping cheaper competitors off the market. An honest supporter would acknowledge this could modestly reduce expected returns on future biologic research.

drawbacks.text: The cap of 20 patents is still a large number, and courts can raise it for good cause, so brand manufacturers retain significant litigation power even after the bill.
The limit does not apply to patents claiming methods of using a biologic drug in therapy or diagnosis, one of the tools commonly used to stretch out patent protection.
The bill's protections only apply to biosimilar applications filed after enactment, so pending disputes are unaffected.

The strongest good-faith objection is that weakening patent enforcement on biologics could reduce the expected return on developing new biologic drugs, since biologics are unusually costly to develop and the patent system is the main way those investments are recouped. Supporters counter that the bill targets litigation volume, not the core patents covering the drug itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a targeted fix to a specific obstacle to biosimilar competition, not a broad price-control law. Its strength is that it works within the existing FDA approval framework and preserves flexibility for courts. Its honest weaknesses are that a cap of 20 patents is still generous, the good-cause exceptions and the carve-out for method-of-use patents let brand makers keep substantial litigation leverage, and it relies on market competition to lower prices rather than setting prices directly, so savings depend on how many biosimilars actually launch.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it unanimously in July 2026, but the House has simply let it sit at the desk without a vote, so nothing has become law yet.

narrative.text: Senator Cornyn introduced the bill in March 2025 with cosponsors from both parties.
The Senate Judiciary Committee reported the bill with amendments in April 2025 and it was placed on the Senate calendar.
The Senate passed the amended bill by unanimous consent on July 21, 2026.
The House received the bill the same day and held it at the desk; it has not been scheduled for a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, brand-name biologic makers are better off: the limit on their patent lawsuits has not taken effect because the House has not acted. Patients waiting for cheaper biosimilars are better off only if the House eventually passes it.

for.name: John Cornyn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and guided it to Senate passage.

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill out of committee with amendments and placed it on the Senate calendar.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill from the Senate on July 21, 2026, and held it at the desk without scheduling a vote; no action since.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator sponsored the bill with Democratic cosponsors, and the Senate passed it by unanimous consent — no senator voted against it — before it stalled at the House desk.

industries.note: They lose the ability to mobilize unlimited patent lists in lawsuits against biosimilar challengers, which shortens the period in which they can charge premium prices for expensive biologic drugs. Patients who need these drugs bear those premium prices today.

With fewer patents to litigate, biosimilar companies face lower legal costs and less risk of drawn-out suits, making it easier to bring lower-priced versions to market. Their interest here runs alongside patients seeking cheaper drugs.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits at the House desk with about five months left in this Congress. Unanimous Senate passage makes floor action simple if House leaders choose it, but bills at the desk at this stage usually die at the end of a Congress unless leadership actively schedules them. If the House does not act, the bill dies and would have to be reintroduced next year.
